question: Is meditation as practiced today allowed, or does it overlap with the rituals of other faiths?
asked: Is meditation, as practiced by modern practitioners, allowed in the Shariah, or is there some overlap with the rituals of other faiths? Many recent studies acknowledge positive results: it helps with mindfulness, stress, focus and wellbeing. What is the Islamic ruling on meditation as it is practiced in our times?
answer:
The answer to this in a nutshell is that there is no doubt that the rituals of another faith are not allowed for us; we may not do anything that is inherently a ritual. For example, to bow down in front of an idol, to show servitude to another god, or to do anything that is uniquely characteristic of another faith, another aqeedah, another religion, that is a symbol of their religion. So for example, it would not be allowed for a Muslim to wear a cross, because that is something that indicates a faith that is against our faith. So clearly anything to do with the rituals or the theology or the specific practices of another religion would not be permissible for us. It would either be haram at the very least, or it might even be a type of kufr and shirk, depending on many other factors.

That is one understanding. At the same time, the cultures, habits and cuisines of any civilization: the default is that these are permissible and halal. And therefore how one dresses, the colors of one's dress, the style of one's dress, the cuisines we eat, the language that we speak, our hand gestures, for example, all of these are cultural, and the Shariah did not come to dictate any one culture over any other culture. This is something we should all know by now.

The issue comes with some aspects that are somewhat in the middle. There are some things that people do that are perhaps a little bit ritual and perhaps a little bit culture. And therefore we need, in those gray areas, to be a little bit more careful and examine what exactly is being asked about.

In this particular instance, the origins of this type of meditation or this practice might, for example, be with certain strands of Buddhism. There's no question that certain religions have a type of meditation that is ritualistic in nature. Now, the question I'm asking you is: the type of meditation that you are practicing, is it completely separate and distinct from what has originated from another faith, and that is meant to achieve a type of enlightenment, i.e. a spiritual journey for the people who practice it? Is it somehow related to that, or is it disconnected from that?

So if a person sits down before going to work for a few minutes and just clears his or her mind and focuses on the day, plans out, "What am I going to be doing?", I don't see any problem with that. At the same time, if you're going to adopt a certain posture and start uttering certain rituals in ancient Sanskrit or whatever, then clearly you have crossed over to something that is ritualistic in nature.

And therefore I would put the question back to you: ask yourself, when you are doing what you are doing, is there an element of another ritual, another faith tradition involved? Or is it simply a means of cleansing your mind and focusing for the day, and making sure that you are better prepared for the day? And if that is the case, then at some level we all meditate. We just take a moment and we begin our task and whatnot; at some level every one of us does that.

Having said that, I would also say that the Shariah has its own mechanisms that are definitely far better. Your question actually reminded me of Ibn Taymiyyah's routine. Ibn al-Qayyim, his famous student, visited him in the early morning, and he said that Ibn Taymiyyah was sitting after Fajr for many hours doing his dhikr and his Qur'an. And when he finished, he turned around and said, "This is my spiritual food. If I don't get my food for the day, I cannot be productive for the rest of the day."

And so we have our own mechanisms. May I suggest to you that the early morning is a time when you should do your Qur'an and some dhikr. Just sit alone, cut off from any noise, any iPhone, anything. Literally sit after Salat al-Fajr, do some Qur'an, do some dhikr, and that "meditation", quote unquote, will be infinitely better and will actually prepare you for the day spiritually and mentally. And that will be in conformity with the Sunnah, because that is exactly what our Prophet did: he would sit after Salat al-Fajr and do his adhkar. And this was the practice of many of the righteous. So I advise you to do that.

Even though, as I said, if you simply cleanse your mind and focus and concentrate, in and of itself, you may call it what you will. All of us do it at a certain level, and **it would be permitted to do that**. And Allah knows best.
